lectures.title: Disaster Management Act, 2005, the National Policy and DRR frameworks

items: **Full name:** The Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Act No. 53 of 2005).
**Background:** enacted after the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami exposed gaps in India's disaster response system.
**Purpose / Objective:** provide a legal and institutional framework for effective management of disasters.

parts.t: Authorities at three levels under the Act
items: **Section 14:** the Governor of a State establishes the State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA).
**AP SDMA Chairperson:** Chief Minister, Andhra Pradesh.
**District level:** the District Magistrate / Collector has overall responsibility.
**SDMA & DDMA (Sections 14 & 25):** State and District level planning & coordination.

parts.t: Bodies and institutions under the Act
items: Assists NDMA; chaired by Home Secretary
Primary fund available with States for immediate relief

parts.t: Nodal ministry and crisis management in the Act sheet
items: **National nodal ministry:** Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
**Nodal responsibility shifted:** from the Department of Agriculture to MHA after the Gujarat earthquake, 2001.
**Nuclear / Biological / Chemical emergencies:** Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS).
For State Capitals and cities with Municipal Corporations
**Statutory status to NCMC & High Level Committee**
Updated definitions of risk, resilience, etc.
**Year:** 2009; approved by the Union Cabinet on 22 October 2009.
**Vision:** to build a safe and disaster-resilient India through a holistic, proactive, multi-disaster oriented and technology-driven strategy.
**Core shift (major paradigm shift):** from a relief-centric approach to prevention, mitigation & preparedness.
**Legal link:** formulated in pursuance of the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
**Global framework guiding India's policy:** Sendai Framework (2015–2030).
India's action-oriented roadmap aligned with Sendai
Operational plan implementing the Policy & Sendai
**Sendai Framework Priority 1:** understanding disaster risk (including hazards).

lectures.title: Ministry of Home Affairs, SDRF, organisations and days

items: **Nodal Ministry:** the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is the nodal ministry for disaster management in India (except drought, pest attack, epidemics, etc.).
**Shifted from:** Department of Agriculture; shifted after the Gujarat Earthquake, 2001.
**Primary responsibility of MHA:** overall coordination of disaster management at the national level.
**Key principle:** primary responsibility lies with State Governments; the Centre (MHA) provides support, coordination & resources.
**Union Government role:** physical & financial resources + early warning + coordination.
**Division concerned:** Disaster Management Division (DM Division) of MHA.
**Nuclear, Biological & Chemical emergencies:** Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS).

parts.t: Functions of the MHA in disaster management
items: Resource mobilisation, coordination of central assistance to states
Operation of National Emergency Operations Centre / Control Room
Matters related to NDRF, SDRF, NDMF & SDMF
Coordination of international assistance & HADR operations
Administrative & budgetary matters of NDMA, NDRF, NIDM
Strengthening of Fire Services, Civil Defence & Home Guards

parts.t: Institutions and their relationship with MHA
items: Administrative control under MHA; policy body chaired by PM
Under MHA; operational control through NDMA
Chaired by Union Home Minister (for financial approvals)
Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change
**Legal basis:** Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Section 44 & related rules).
**Nature:** State-level specialised response force (counterpart of NDRF).
**Primary role:** first responder within the state (first 24–48 hours).
**Training:** trained by NDRF / NDRF Academy on similar standards.
**Composition:** drawn mainly from State Police, Armed Police, Fire Services, Home Guards, Civil Defence.
**Structure:** organised on battalion model (similar to NDRF); multi-disciplinary teams.
**Specialisation:** Search & Rescue, Flood rescue, Collapsed structure, CBRN (in some states).
**Purpose:** primary fund available with States for immediate relief to victims of notified disasters.
**Administered by:** State Executive Committee (SEC) headed by Chief Secretary.
**Notified disasters:** Cyclone, Drought, Earthquake, Fire, Flood, Tsunami, Hailstorm, Landslide, Avalanche, Cloudburst, Pest Attack, Frost & Cold Wave.
**Additional flexibility:** up to 10% of SDRF can be used for State-specific disasters (not in notified list).
**Limitation:** used only for immediate relief, not for compensation of individual losses or long-term reconstruction.
Apex body for disaster management (chaired by PM)
Premier DM capacity-development institute; capacity building, training & research
**NDRF Regional HQ for AP, Telangana & Karnataka**
Remote sensing; remote sensing support for disasters
**United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR)**
Focal point for Sendai Framework & global DRR
Disaster awareness & local capabilities; regional capacity building in Asia
International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction (IDDRR)
Global day to promote a culture of disaster risk reduction and resilience; core global DRR awareness day
Honours humanitarian workers and those affected by crises
Highlights the role of weather, climate and water services in disaster risk reduction
Links environment degradation with increased disaster risk
**NDMA Formation Day:** observed on 28 September (NDMA was notified in 2006).
**Mock Exercises & Awareness Campaigns:** conducted regularly by NDMA, NIDM, NDRF and State authorities throughout the year.

lectures.title: Classification of hazards and GIS in disaster management

items: Cyclone; Flood; Drought; Thunderstorm-related hazards; Hailstorm
Fire; Industrial/chemical disasters; Nuclear disasters; Biological disasters
**High Powered Committee (1999):** classified disasters into 5 broad categories.
**Key approach:** from hazard-centric to multi-hazard risk reduction.

parts.t: Hazards: broad categories, sub-types and examples
items: Drought, Heat wave, Cold wave, Forest fire
Industrial accidents, Chemical leaks, Nuclear accidents, Dam failure
**Socio-Natural Hazards:** combination of natural + human factors; e.g. floods worsened by deforestation, landslides due to unscientific construction.
**GIS in Disaster Management:** a tool for disaster management.
**Main function:** store, manipulate, analyse and present geographical data.
**Disaster mapping:** Remote Sensing + GIS + Satellite Data.
**Advanced application:** modelling & analysing spatial data and displaying community vulnerability.

parts.t: GIS applications across the disaster management cycle
items: Hazard zonation mapping, vulnerability assessment, risk mapping, land-use planning
Evacuation route planning, resource mapping, early warning system support
Real-time damage assessment, search & rescue coordination, resource allocation
Damage assessment, "Build Back Better" planning, monitoring reconstruction
Flood inundation mapping, floodplain zoning, real-time monitoring
Track monitoring, storm surge modelling, evacuation planning
Seismic hazard zonation, damage assessment using pre/post images

parts.t: Organisations and platforms for GIS-based disaster management
items: Decision Support Centre; provides satellite-based inputs
ISRO's geoportal for visualisation and analysis
Use GIS for planning, decision support and guidelines
Unified geospatial database for emergency management

corrections.checked: The Bill was passed by the Rajya Sabha on 28 November 2005 and the Lok Sabha on 12 December 2005; 23 December 2005 is the date of Presidential assent, not of passing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster_Management_Act,_2005)
